the role of cell-cell adhesion in Drosophila wing disc development.
the molecular mechanisms of Drosophilla wing development, and the roles of the ap and Fng genes in this process.
the mechanisms of compartmentalization in the Drosophila wing disc.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
dorsal identity is not required for Drosophila wing vein formation and that inter-compamental signaling, mediated through Fng, is the key factor in maintaining the Drosophila D/V boundary.

the dorsal identity of the wing is not necessary to maintain the D/V boundary and to pattern the wing margin, and that the dorsal compartment is maintained in the absence of ap expression by the combined effects of the integrin and Fng.
the D/V compartment boundary is not established and maintained by a single mechanism, but by a number of different mechanisms, each of which is essential for proper wing development.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

dorsal identity is not required for wing development, that the dorsal compartment boundary is established and maintained by inter-compartmental signals and that a limited number of downstream targets of ap mediate the full range of Ap function.
Drosophila wing disc development can occur in the absence of Ap function and that D/V compartmental boundary formation and maintenance are not essential for wing development.
the Drosophila wing disc has the capacity to develop in the absence of the dorsal compartment.
The main takeaway from our work is that
D/V compartmental boundaries in Drosophila wings are maintained by inter-compartment signaling, and not by differential cell adhesion.

a relatively small number of genes are responsible for the establishment and maintenance of the dorsal compartment boundary and that the dorsal compartment identity is not essential for the development of the adult dorsal structures.
the dorsal compartment is not necessary for wing formation, and that the dorsal compartment boundary is not maintained by a simple mechanism of cell adhesion.
